Supplementary Table 2: Calibration compares modelled first-year rates with GBD 2023 targets in every country, sex and five-year age group, for the four-state life table and for the full model with each state divided by diabetes status. The external plausibility check simulated a cohort with the composition of SELECT participants by qualifying disease, age and sex over 40 months, using rates calibrated to GBD 2023 rather than trial data. These rates applied to all people living with IHD or IS, not only to those without diabetes or with a BMI of 27 or more, and the comparison is with the cardiovascular death end point of the SELECT placebo group, which also includes deaths from heart failure, arrhythmia and undetermined causes. Persistence reconstruction compares the cumulative discontinuation and reinitiation at one and two years implied by the model with the values published by Rodriguez et al (2025). The annual coverage check reports how far enrolment carried over from the previous year exceeded the target, because places were freed only by death. The BMI rows compare the estimated share of adults with BMI of 27 or more under the log-normal distribution (main analysis) and a gamma distribution. Population conservation error was below 1e-15 in every country, sex and age (not tabulated). BMI, body mass index; CV, cardiovascular; GBD, Global Burden of Disease. This comparison checks that the modelled magnitude is plausible and is not a formal external validation, because the populations and end points are not fully matched. *Rodriguez PJ, Zhang V, Gratzl S, et al. Discontinuation and reinitiation of dual-labeled GLP-1 receptor agonists among US adults with overweight or obesity. JAMA Netw Open 2025;8:e2457349.
Supplementary Table 3: Each of 1000 simulations drew one value of every parameter. Hazard ratios were drawn from log-normal distributions matching their 95% confidence intervals, and the other parameters from the distributions shown. The same 1000 draws were used in every analysis (common random numbers), so differences between scenarios reflect the scenario rather than sampling. Dietary effects were multiplied by an outcome-specific factor, fitted to the GBD 2023 95% uncertainty interval of the diet-attributable fraction relative to its point estimate, common to all countries within each draw and drawn independently for each outcome. The centiles summarise the values drawn. Dietary multipliers were drawn independently for each outcome because GBD 2023 estimates the dose-response uncertainty separately for each outcome, and were shared across countries because the same dose-response curves apply to every country. CKD, chronic kidney disease; CV, cardiovascular; HR, hazard ratio; IHD, ischaemic heart disease; MI, myocardial infarction; SBP, systolic blood pressure; T2D, type 2 diabetes.
Supplementary Table 4: Deaths attributable to all dietary risks jointly (GBD 2023 "Dietary risks" estimates), adults aged 25 years and older, both sexes. Deaths and uncertainty intervals were summed across age and sex groups. Joint estimates can be negative or have negative lower bounds where GBD estimates protective associations for some factors, such as red meat. Crude rates use the population aged 25 years and older. Age-standardised rates use the 2023 GBD global population aged 25 years and older as the standard; the global age-standardised rate therefore equals the crude rate. Global refers to the GBD 2023 global estimate, not the sum of the 19 study countries. The burden by dietary factor (next table) uses single-factor estimates, which exceed the joint burden where factors overlap.
Supplementary Table 5: Deaths from IHD and ischaemic stroke attributable to each dietary factor separately among adults aged 25 years or older in 2023 (GBD 2023 single-factor estimates). Single-factor estimates are not additive, because the joint burden accounts for overlap between factors. These values give the dietary composition of the burden and the share targeted by the feasible package (sodium, whole grains and sugar-sweetened beverages). Negative single-factor estimates, which GBD 2023 gives for red meat and some stroke types, were counted as zero for each outcome. CV, cardiovascular; GBD, Global Burden of Disease; IHD, ischaemic heart disease.
Supplementary Table 6: Medians and 95% uncertainty intervals from 1000 simulations. Treatment coverage is the share of eligible adults enrolled, maintained for 30 years, with places offered first to adults with IHD or ischaemic stroke and BMI ≥27 or diabetes, then to adults with diabetes at any BMI, then to adults with BMI ≥30. Maximum affordable coverage is the share of income quintiles for which the generic annual cost (US$140) is within 10% of per-capita income. Dietary policy effects do not depend on treatment coverage. Both interventions together assume independent action, the upper end of the range of combined benefit considered. Dietary effects on CKD act through sodium intake and blood pressure only. In Nigeria, baseline sodium intake was below 3.0 g/day, below which no benefit of further reduction was modelled, so the feasible package produced no modelled reduction in CKD deaths. The aspirational scenario moves all 12 dietary factors 20% towards their TMREL. Which intervention averted more deaths was judged from the diet-to-treatment ratio computed within each simulation, which can differ from a comparison of the two medians. In the United States at 10% coverage, for example, the median ratio was 0.96, although the median deaths averted were 268.1 thousand for dietary policy and 257.4 thousand for treatment. BMI, body mass index; CKD, chronic kidney disease; IHD, ischaemic heart disease; UI, uncertainty interval.
Supplementary Table 7: Crossover coverage is the coverage of eligible adults at which GLP-1RA treatment would avert as many deaths from IHD and ischaemic stroke over 30 years as the feasible dietary package. Where treatment averted fewer deaths than dietary policy even with every eligible adult enrolled, crossover is reported as not reached, and treatment at full coverage gives the deaths averted by treatment with every eligible adult enrolled as a percentage of those averted by dietary policy. Probabilities are the share of 1000 simulations in which dietary policy averted more deaths. The overtaking year is the first year in which dietary policy averted more deaths per year than treatment, from median annual trajectories. Treatment at full coverage is the deaths averted with every eligible adult enrolled, as a percentage of those averted by the feasible package. Adults eligible in year 1 are those meeting the eligibility criteria at the start of the projection. IHD, ischaemic heart disease; UI, uncertainty interval.
Supplementary Table 8: At 0% overlap the two interventions act independently on each person's risk, applied multiplicatively in the life table with competing risks, so that no death is counted twice. With partial overlap the combined benefit is reduced by that proportion of its excess over the larger single intervention, and at 100% the combination averts as many deaths or cases as the more effective intervention alone. The added benefit is the extra deaths or cases averted by adding dietary policy to treatment, as a percentage of treatment alone and as the combination's multiple of treatment alone. Under complete overlap the multiple equals the diet-to-treatment ratio where dietary policy averts more, and 1 where treatment does. Medians and 95% uncertainty intervals from 1000 simulations, with multiples computed within each simulation. Within each simulation, the combination under independent action averted slightly fewer deaths than the sum of the two interventions alone, because they partly act on the same people. Its median can nonetheless exceed the sum of the separate medians, because medians are not additive. CKD, chronic kidney disease; IHD, ischaemic heart disease; UI, uncertainty interval.
Supplementary Table 9: Crossover coverage is the treatment coverage at which treatment and the feasible dietary package avert the same number of incident type 2 diabetes cases or CKD deaths over 30 years, and ratios are dietary policy to treatment, computed within each of 1000 simulations. Where treatment averted fewer cases or deaths than dietary policy even with every eligible adult enrolled, crossover is reported as not reached. Treatment prevents diabetes only in enrolled adults without diabetes, so its benefit is small at coverage levels filled mainly by adults with cardiovascular disease or diabetes. Dietary effects on CKD act through sodium intake and blood pressure only. In Nigeria, baseline sodium intake was below 3.0 g/day, below which no benefit of further reduction was modelled, so the feasible package produced no modelled reduction in CKD deaths, and the diet-to-treatment ratio is zero. CKD, chronic kidney disease; UI, uncertainty interval.
Supplementary Table 10: Medians and 95% uncertainty intervals from 1000 simulations. Each factor was shifted 20% toward its TMREL alone in the dietary policy arm, with the other factors held at observed intake. The share of the country benefit is each factor's share of the summed single-factor benefit, computed within each simulation. Single-factor results are not additive. Sodium-related risk is counted only above 3.0 g a day (the midpoint of the GBD 2023 TMREL interval); modelled sodium intake in Nigeria is below this level, so sodium reduction has no modelled benefit there. IHD, ischaemic heart disease; TMREL, theoretical minimum risk exposure level; UI, uncertainty interval.
Supplementary Table 11: Medians and 95% uncertainty intervals from 1000 simulations per scenario, using the same draws as the main analysis. Crossover coverage in the scenarios is interpolated between 11 coverage levels, and in the main analysis between 27. Where treatment averted fewer deaths than dietary policy even with every eligible adult enrolled, crossover is reported as not reached. In the scenario restricted to adults resembling the SELECT population, treatment's benefit was close to zero in some simulations, because the SELECT confidence interval for cardiovascular death included no effect, so this scenario is summarised as treatment's deaths averted as a percentage of those averted by dietary policy. In the discounting scenario, deaths in later years were discounted at 3% a year. The scenario in which every eligible adult with IHD or IS was enrolled from year 2 was run at 20% starting coverage only, so no crossover coverage was estimated. In Nigeria, modelled sodium intake is below 3.0 g a day, so a 30% sodium reduction averts no deaths. Its crossover is shown as no modelled dietary benefit, its diet-to-treatment ratio is zero, and treatment as a percentage of the dietary benefit is not estimable. Where the treatment benefit was close to or below zero in some simulations, the median diet-to-treatment ratio is shown but its 95% uncertainty interval is not estimable, and the treatment benefit as a percentage of the dietary benefit can be read instead, and where the dietary benefit was close to zero the percentage is not estimable. In the scenarios that change stopping, the stopping multiplier was fixed at the stated value in every simulation, in place of the range of 0.75 to 1.25 used in the main analysis. UI, uncertainty interval.
Supplementary Table 12: Stopping probabilities were multiplied by 0 (nobody stops), 0.5, 1 or 1.5, combined with dietary policy effects held at 100%, 80%, 60% or 40% of their full size throughout follow-up and with phase-in over 8, 12 or 16 years. Medians and 95% uncertainty intervals from 1000 simulations per scenario, at 20% treatment coverage. In each simulation, the stopping multiplier was fixed at the value shown, whereas the main analysis varies it between 0.75 and 1.25 across simulations. The combination of 100% dietary policy effect, stopping multiplier 1 and an 8-year phase-in therefore corresponds to the main analysis without uncertainty in stopping, and differs slightly from it. UI, uncertainty interval.
Supplementary Table 14: Education-specific PAFs were estimated by applying within-country dietary exposure gradients from the GDD to national GBD 2023 exposure estimates. Values are percentages of all deaths (or incident cases for T2D) from each outcome attributable to dietary risk in each education group. Education groups were low (no education, incomplete primary or primary), medium (lower or upper secondary) and high (post-secondary or above).
Supplementary Table 15: Attributable deaths in each education group were allocated from the national total in proportion to the group PAF multiplied by the group population share, that is, deaths in group g = national attributable deaths x PAF(g) x share(g) / sum over groups of PAF x share. Population shares by education group were derived from the Wittgenstein Centre Human Capital Data Explorer for adults aged 25 and over. This approximation assumes equal age-specific mortality rates across education groups; differences arise entirely from the PAF and population structure. Total attributable deaths are from GBD 2023. Attributable deaths in each group are reported in thousands.
Supplementary Table 16: Per-capita income by quintile was estimated from World Bank income quintile shares (2022-2024) multiplied by GNI per capita (Atlas method, 2025). Branded prices are those paid by a self-paying patient for semaglutide 2.4 mg, one pen of four weekly doses, accessed in October 2026 (Canada, telephone survey in June 2026), with 13 pens a year, and were converted to US dollars at European Central Bank reference rates of 26 October 2026 (Brazil, 23 October 2026, and Egypt, the approximate official rate). Prices were taken from official price lists where available and otherwise from pharmacy or clinic retail prices, including value added tax where it applies. In Bangladesh and Nigeria, where the drug has not been launched, prices were imputed. Generic price bounds (US$140 a year upper, US$28 a year lower) are from a production-cost analysis (Levi et al, Obesity 2026). Affordability was defined as an annual treatment cost not exceeding 10% of estimated per-capita income within each income quintile. This study-specific threshold is not a measure of catastrophic health expenditure under WHO definitions, which relate household out-of-pocket health spending to household consumption or discretionary budget. Income quintile Q1 is the poorest 20% and Q5 is the richest 20%. IND and NGA quintile incomes are derived from consumption surveys and may conservatively overestimate affordability for Q1-Q2. Price sources: Australia, Pharmacy retail price (not listed on the PBS); Bangladesh, Not launched; imputed as the price in India, the nearest launched market; Brazil, Pharmacy retail price (single pen); regulated maximum consumer price (CMED PMC, ICMS 18%) BRL 2,532.31; Bulgaria, National Council on Prices and Reimbursement register (maximum retail price); Canada, Median of three national pharmacy chains, cash price including dispensing fee (telephone survey, June 2026); China, Provincial procurement listing price, Qinghai and Shanghai (identical); Egypt, Pharmacy retail price; Germany, Pharmacy retail price (Apothekenverkaufspreis) from 1 April 2026; India, Novo Nordisk India price list effective 1 April 2026 (maximum retail price); Israel, Consumer list price at a health fund pharmacy (Leumit); halved for supplementary insurance members meeting medical criteria; Japan, Self-pay clinic price, two clinics (identical); reimbursed price JPY 40,861; Mexico, Pharmacy regular retail price; New Zealand, Pharmacy non-subsidised retail price (not funded by Pharmac); Nigeria, Not launched; imputed as the mean price in Egypt and South Africa, the launched markets in Africa; Romania, National public catalogue of maximum medicine prices (CaNaMed); South Africa, Single exit price, Medicine Price Registry database of 1 October 2026 (excludes dispensing fee); Türkiye, Retail price from the national medicines price list (TITCK), via Ilac Rehberi; United Kingdom, Private online pharmacy price (MedExpress); NHS list price GBP 175.80 excluding VAT; United States of America, NovoCare Pharmacy self-pay price (one month defined as one box of 4 pens). GNI, gross national income; GLP-1RA, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist.
Supplementary Table 17: Deaths averted in each five-year age group were allocated to education groups using the education structure of that age group (Wittgenstein Centre), so that the older and less educated age profile of cardiovascular deaths is reflected. Within each age group, deaths averted by dietary policy were allocated in proportion to each group's population share multiplied by its diet-attributable fraction, and deaths averted by treatment in proportion to population share multiplied by the fraction of the group able to afford treatment, defined by income quintiles for which the annual cost is within 10% of per-capita income, with education groups placed on the income percentile scale in rank order. Treatment at 20% coverage of eligible adults. Medians and 95% uncertainty intervals from 1000 simulations of the main analysis, with education-specific PAFs, population shares, affordability and the education-income link at central values, and ratios computed within each simulation. Totals cover the 19 countries only and exclude the rest of the world. In the United Kingdom, fewer than 0.1% of adults aged 25 years or older were classified as low education, so its low-education estimates are not interpretable. Rows for the 19 countries combined sum deaths averted across countries within each simulation, and shares are the percentage of the dietary policy benefit occurring in each education group, also computed within each simulation. GLP-1RA, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist; PAF, population attributable fraction.
Supplementary Table 18: Medians and 95% uncertainty intervals from 1000 simulations of the main analysis, with ratios computed within each simulation. Deaths averted over 30 years in the low-education group at the generic price of US$140 a year and 20% treatment coverage, with education and income perfectly ranked (main analysis), partly linked (50%), or unrelated.
Supplementary Table 19: Medians and 95% uncertainty intervals from 1000 simulations, with costs and deaths undiscounted or discounted at 3% a year (mid-year). Deaths averted and person-years on treatment both come from each simulation, with prices fixed, and ratios are computed within each simulation. In one of the 1000 simulations, treatment averted no deaths in some countries because the sampled hazard ratios were above 1, and its expenditure per death averted was then counted as unbounded. Treatment expenditure counts only person-time on drug, given stopping and restarting. Dietary policy implementation costs US$0.55 per adult per year (sodium reformulation, taxation of sugar-sweetened beverages and whole-grain promotion). Deaths averted are from IHD and ischaemic stroke, and with CKD added, over 30 years. Expenditure covers only the drug cost for time on treatment and the implementation cost of the dietary package, from a public payer perspective, in US dollars, with branded prices converted at exchange rates of October 2026 and unit costs held constant over 30 years. It excludes delivery, monitoring, adverse events and downstream health-care costs and savings, so it is not a full cost-effectiveness analysis. CKD, chronic kidney disease; IHD, ischaemic heart disease.
Supplementary Table 20: Medians and 95% uncertainty intervals from 1000 simulations. Deaths averted and person-years on treatment both come from each simulation, with prices fixed, and ratios are computed within each simulation. Expenditure was calculated with treatment paying only for time on drug and dietary policy costing US$0.55 per adult per year, over 30 years without discounting. Deaths are deaths from IHD and ischaemic stroke averted over 30 years. Panel A, the GLP-1RA coverage of eligible adults whose 30-year expenditure equals the cost of the dietary package, the deaths it would avert, and the ratio of deaths averted by the dietary package to those averted by that treatment. Panel B, the expenditure of treatment at 20% coverage spent on treatment alone, or on the dietary package first with the remainder on treatment, using the combination of the two under independent action. Coverage was not limited to the maximum affordable level, because the programme is assumed to be publicly financed, and deaths were interpolated between the coverage levels of the Monte Carlo analysis. GLP-1RA, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist; IHD, ischaemic heart disease; UI, uncertainty interval.
Supplementary Table 21: Medians and 95% uncertainty intervals from 1000 simulations. The ratio is the number of deaths from IHD and ischaemic stroke averted over 30 years per dollar spent on the feasible dietary package, divided by the number averted per dollar spent on GLP-1RA treatment at 20% coverage of eligible adults, and was computed within each simulation. It equals the ratio of treatment to dietary policy expenditure per death averted, and is also the factor by which the cost of the dietary package could rise before treatment averted more deaths per dollar. A ratio above 1 indicates that dietary policy averted more deaths per dollar. Expenditure was calculated with treatment paying only for time on drug and dietary policy costing US$0.55 per adult per year, over 30 years without discounting, with prices fixed. Branded prices are country-specific, so no global estimate is given for them. GLP-1RA, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist; IHD, ischaemic heart disease; UI, uncertainty interval.
Supplementary Table 22: Medians and 95% uncertainty intervals from 1000 simulations, global totals over 30 years, in thousands; ratios are computed within each simulation. Relative risk of diabetes incidence of 0.26 (GLP-1RA node of a network meta-analysis in prediabetes) and 0.10 (dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist node of the same analysis, based on a single trial, SURMOUNT-1, low certainty), against a hazard ratio of 0.27 in the main analysis (SELECT). Blood pressure falls of 3.31 mmHg (SELECT), 5.10 mmHg (STEP 1), 6.32 mmHg (meta-analysis in adults without diabetes) and none in adults with diabetes or in all adults, against 3.80 and 2.13 mmHg by diabetes status in the main analysis. Treatment affects CKD only through blood pressure, so without a blood pressure fall it averts no CKD deaths. CKD, chronic kidney disease; GIP, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide; GLP-1RA, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist; HR, hazard ratio; RR, relative risk; SBP, systolic blood pressure; T2D, type 2 diabetes.
Supplementary Table 13: Education-specific PAFs were estimated by applying within-country dietary exposure gradients from the Global Dietary Database (GDD) to national exposure estimates from GBD 2023 and passing the adjusted exposures through the same dose-response framework. Ratios are low-education PAFs divided by high-education PAFs, with 95% uncertainty intervals from 1000 Monte Carlo draws over the GDD exposure distributions. Dose-response curves were held fixed, so these intervals reflect uncertainty in the education gradient only and are not comparable with the intervals of the main analysis. Upper bounds above 100, where the high-education PAF approaches zero, are reported as not estimable. A ratio above 1.0 indicates higher diet-attributable burden in the low-education group. Education strata were low (no education, incomplete primary or primary), medium (lower or upper secondary) and high (post-secondary, bachelor, master or higher), as defined by the GDD. Educational gradients for CKD are less stable than for the other outcomes. For CKD, the upper bound in Bangladesh is not estimable because the high-education PAF approaches zero in some draws. Dietary effects on CKD act through sodium only, and baseline sodium intake in Nigeria was below 3.0 g/day, below which no benefit of further reduction was modelled, so there is no modelled dietary benefit for CKD in Nigeria.
